wrong_answers: Leap sideways to break its scent trail
hints: Hares trust their legs more than hiding places.
Their cousins, rabbits, are the ones who live in tunnels.
Hares sleep in a shallow dip on the open ground.
questions.fun_fact: Baby hares are born with fur and open eyes in a shallow nest on the ground, while baby rabbits are born bare and blind in burrows.

questions.description: An animal that would win any contest for doing nothing.
questions.question: “I'm the slowest mammal on Earth, I hang upside down in trees and I sleep most of the day.” Where do I live?
hints: I need lots of trees and warm weather.
It rains almost every day where I live.
My home is near the Amazon River.
questions.fun_fact: Sloths move so slowly that tiny green algae grow in their fur, helping them hide among the leaves.

Gliders and paragliders use the same trick.

It can live longer than ten mice in a row.
questions.fun_fact: Naked mole-rats hardly ever get cancer and can survive for minutes without oxygen.

questions.question: Jupiter is a gas giant. About how many Earths could fit inside it?
hints: Jupiter is the biggest planet in the solar system.
About 11 Earths would fit side by side across Jupiter.
Eleven times wider means about 11 × 11 × 11 times the space inside.
questions.fun_fact: Jupiter has no solid ground: if you tried to land on it, you would just sink into thicker and thicker gas.

questions.description: The Moon has a bumpy face because space keeps throwing rocks at it.

hints: The Moon is covered with thousands of me.
You can see some of me with binoculars.
If you drop a stone into sand, you make a tiny copy of me.
questions.fun_fact: Because the Moon has no wind or rain, astronaut footprints there can last for millions of years.

hints: My discovery in 2005 started a big debate among astronomers.
That debate ended with Pluto no longer being a planet.
In myth, I threw a golden apple that led to the Trojan War.
questions.fun_fact: Eris is about the same size as Pluto but more massive, and its moon is named Dysnomia, the daughter of strife.

hints: It is a gas giant.
It is the second-biggest planet.
It is the one famous for its huge rings.
questions.fun_fact: In a bathtub big enough to hold it, Saturn would float, though it would leave a ring!

media.author: Thomas Tolkien from Yorkshire, UK

questions.description: Not ice cream, not icebergs, but giants made of ice.
questions.question: How many planets in our solar system are ice giants?
hints: Ice giants are smaller than Jupiter and Saturn, but much bigger than Earth.
Ice giants are the farthest planets from the Sun.
Uranus is one, and it spins tipped on its side.
questions.fun_fact: The “ice” in ice giants is mostly water, ammonia and methane, and it is not cold at all deep inside.

hints: He flew on Apollo 17, the final Moon landing.
He was the commander of his mission, and his partner was a geologist.
His first name is a short form of Eugene.
questions.fun_fact: Before leaving, Gene Cernan wrote his daughter's initials in the Moon dust.

questions.description: A shoe print that's very far from your front door.
questions.question: This famous footprint was not made on Earth. Who left it?
hints: The gray dust in the photo is on the Moon.
This person needed a rocket to get there.
They wear a big white suit and a helmet.
questions.fun_fact: There is no wind or rain on the Moon, so footprints there can last for millions of years.

hints: Its makers say it was made for people on a very long trip.
Those people traveled far above the clouds.
They wear helmets and ride rockets.
questions.fun_fact: This freeze-dried ice cream was made for NASA, but astronauts almost never ate it in space, because its crumbs could float into equipment.

hints: The station is much faster than Earth's spin.
It flies around the whole Earth many times a day.
They see about 16 sunrises in a single day.
questions.fun_fact: The station travels at about 28,000 km/h (17,500 mph), fast enough to circle Earth in about an hour and a half.

In English they are often named after the place where rockets go.
questions.fun_fact: The foil blanket is so thin that it can be folded to the size of a wallet, yet it reflects most of your body heat back to you.

Spacewalks are planned like a long work shift.
It's longer than a school morning, but shorter than a whole day.
questions.fun_fact: NASA's official name for the space diaper is “Maximum Absorbency Garment”.

He launched from Baikonur, the same place as Yuri Gagarin.
questions.fun_fact: Dennis Tito spent about eight days in space and later said it was “paradise”.

It's the gas that makes up most of the air you breathe.

It is meant to be a whole system, not one ship.
The first word is the place where it goes.

hints: Every astronaut needs me several times a day.
I have a seat.
On Earth, you flush me.
questions.fun_fact: On the space station, urine is cleaned and turned back into drinking water.

The people here can be on duty day and night until the crew is safely home.
The astronauts call this room “Houston” in many films.
questions.fun_fact: During the Apollo 13 emergency, mission control teams worked day and night to bring the crew safely home.

It circles the whole Earth in about 90 minutes.
People live and work inside it.
questions.fun_fact: The International Space Station is big enough that you can see it without a telescope from almost anywhere on Earth.

You use it to make tacos and burritos.
questions.fun_fact: Floating crumbs can get into astronauts' eyes or into machines, so bread is rarely eaten in space.

questions.description: The universe is getting bigger, and it's not because of all the snacks.
questions.question: “In 1929, I used the redshift of galaxies' light to show that they're flying away from us.” Who am I?

A famous space telescope launched in 1990 carries his name.

My name sounds like a bag of black fuel for a fireplace.
questions.fun_fact: Some Aboriginal Australians see the Coalsack as the head of an “emu in the sky” made of dark clouds.

Its color name is the same as snow.
questions.fun_fact: Planetary nebulas got their name because, in old telescopes, they looked round like planets.

Its name is the Latin word for maiden.

questions.description: The most important royal seat isn't even comfortable.
questions.question: I'm a block of sandstone that Scottish kings were crowned on. Students took me from London at Christmas 1950. What am I?
hints: Today I'm shown in a museum in Perth, Scotland.
Edward I carried me off to England in 1296.
My other name is the Stone of Destiny.
questions.fun_fact: The stone traveled back to London for Charles III's coronation in 2023 and sat inside the old Coronation Chair.

media.credit: Robert Lamb · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Robert Lamb

questions.description: Millions of viewers, one very long aisle, and nobody tripped on the dress.
questions.question: I'm a London church. In 2011, Prince William and Catherine Middleton got married under my roof. Where am I?
hints: Kings and queens have been crowned here since 1066.
I stand right next to the Houses of Parliament.
Isaac Newton and Charles Darwin are buried inside me.
questions.fun_fact: For the wedding, rows of real trees were placed inside the church along the aisle.

media.credit: Richard Humphrey · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Richard Humphrey

questions.description: A crown that comes with the wedding ring, but not with the job.
questions.question: She is married to the king and crowned with him, but she doesn't rule. Camilla has had this title since 2022. What is it?
hints: The title comes from her marriage.
A queen who rules in her own right is called “regnant”.
The second word also means “partner”.
questions.fun_fact: Queen Victoria's husband, Albert, was officially given the title “Prince Consort” in 1857.

media.credit: Dennis G. Jarvis · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dennis G. Jarvis

questions.description: A family that changed its surname to match its favorite castle.
questions.question: Which of these royals was NOT part of the House of Windsor?
hints: The Windsor name was only created in 1917.
The odd one out ruled in the 1800s.
She was Elizabeth II's great-great-grandmother.
questions.fun_fact: The family took the name Windsor in 1917 because the old name, Saxe-Coburg and Gotha, sounded too German during World War I.

media.credit: Diliff · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Diliff

questions.description: The most famous face you've ever kept in your pocket.
questions.question: You find a coin with Elizabeth II's profile on it. Roughly how many countries have put her face on their money?
hints: Canada, Australia and New Zealand are among them.
Many of them were once British colonies.
It's more than 30, but fewer than 50.
questions.fun_fact: Guinness World Records lists her as the person shown on the most different currencies.

media.credit: Windrain · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Windrain

questions.description: A zoo painted across the night sky, with a few strange guests.
questions.question: Horoscopes use twelve star patterns that the Sun seems to pass through during the year. What are they called together?
hints: Their names are very old and come from Latin and Greek.
Most of them are named after animals, like the lion and the bull.
People ask “What's your sign?” based on your birthday.
questions.fun_fact: The word “zodiac” comes from Greek and means something like “circle of little animals”.

media.credit: Chad Ajamian · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Chad Ajamian

questions.description: Love that is worth more than its weight in metal.
questions.question: A silver wedding anniversary marks 25 years of marriage. How many years does a golden one mark?
hints: Gold is worth more than silver, so it takes longer.
It's half a century.
Double the silver one.
questions.fun_fact: After 60 years of marriage, couples celebrate a diamond anniversary.

media.credit: Petar Milošević · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Petar Milošević

questions.description: The only clock that waits for you to say “go!”.
questions.question: I start when you press my button, I stop when you press it again, and I time running races at school. What am I?
hints: I measure time very exactly, even parts of a second.
Coaches often hang me around their neck.
I'm a small handheld timer with a big button on top, and many phones have one built in.
questions.fun_fact: In top races, the time is measured to a hundredth of a second, so two runners can be just 0.01 seconds apart.

media.credit: 褒忠國中 雲端網 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: 褒忠國中 雲端網

questions.description: Not yesterday, but the yesterday of yesterday.
questions.question: Today is Wednesday and yesterday was Tuesday. What day was the day before yesterday?
hints: Go back two days.
It's the first day of the school week in many countries.
It comes right after Sunday.
questions.fun_fact: Some languages have a single word for it, like Spanish “anteayer” and German “vorgestern”.

media.credit: Claudio Elias · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Claudio Elias

questions.description: The week is a merry-go-round that always comes back.
questions.question: If today is Sunday, how many days is it until the next Sunday?
hints: Count the days of one whole week.
Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday…
It's the same as the number of days in a week.
questions.fun_fact: The seven-day week is thousands of years old and goes back to ancient Babylon.

media.credit: Ruth Sharville · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ruth Sharville

questions.description: A riddle that fits in your planner.
questions.question: Monday is to the week as September is to the…
hints: Monday is one part of a week.
September is one of twelve.
It starts on January 1.
questions.fun_fact: September comes from the Latin word for seven, because it was the seventh month in the old Roman calendar.

media.credit: Shixart1985 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Shixart1985

questions.description: Every year number on your phone starts counting from me.
questions.question: I'm the event that the world's most used calendar counts its years from. What am I?
hints: The years before me are counted backwards.
A monk worked me out about 1,500 years ago.
It's remembered every year at Christmas.
questions.fun_fact: The monk who set up the count probably got it slightly wrong: historians think Jesus was born a few years “before Christ”.

media.credit: EgorovaSvetlana · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: EgorovaSvetlana

questions.description: The day ties get wrapped and pancakes get burned.
questions.question: I'm a day when children give their dads cards, hugs and breakfast in bed. What am I?
hints: I'm not about moms.
Many countries celebrate me in June.
I'm the dad's own day.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain and Italy, Father's Day is on March 19, the feast of Saint Joseph.

media.credit: keyaki · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: keyaki

questions.description: The day that already happened, and you can't take it back.
questions.question: Complete it: “Today is Monday, so yesterday was…”
hints: Yesterday is the day before today.
It comes right after Saturday.
It comes right before Monday.
questions.fun_fact: Many weekday names come from the Sun, the Moon and the planets known in ancient times, so in English Sunday is the Sun's day and Monday is the Moon's day.

media.credit: Claudio Elias · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Claudio Elias

questions.description: The only castle guest who never needs a door.
questions.question: I float through castle walls at night and shout “Boo!”. In cartoons, what am I usually made of?
hints: You can make this costume at home for a party.
You can find it on a bed.
Cut two holes for the eyes and put it over your head!
questions.fun_fact: In Mario games, the shy ghost called Boo hides its face whenever you look at it.

media.credit: Michael Gaylard from Horsham, UK · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Michael Gaylard from Horsham, UK

questions.description: A Swiss castle with a lake view, a cold dungeon and one very famous visitor.
questions.question: I stand on a rock in Lake Geneva, in Switzerland. A famous poet wrote about a prisoner chained in my dungeon. Who was that poet?
hints: He visited in 1816, the famous “Year Without a Summer”.
The real prisoner was François Bonivard, who was locked up there in the 1530s.
This English poet wrote “Don Juan” and was the father of Ada Lovelace.
questions.fun_fact: Visitors can still see the name “Byron” carved into a pillar of the dungeon, but no one knows for sure whether he carved it himself.

media.credit: Ank Kumar · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ank Kumar

questions.description: The medieval living room, dining room and bedroom, all in one drafty space.
questions.question: I was the biggest room in a medieval castle. The lord held feasts in me, and some servants slept on my floor. What am I?
hints: Everyone in the castle came here to eat together.
A long table and a huge fireplace were often my main features.
At Hogwarts, the students eat in a room with this name.
questions.fun_fact: Westminster Hall in London, finished in 1099, was one of the largest halls in Europe when it was built.

media.credit: Scotch Mist · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Scotch Mist

questions.description: Proof that you should never judge a friend by their size.
questions.question: A lion lets a tiny mouse go free. Later, the lion gets caught in a hunter's net. What does the mouse do?
hints: The mouse uses something it has in its mouth.
The mouse helps all by itself, with no other animals and without making a sound.
Its sharp little teeth bite the net open.
questions.fun_fact: This fable is often credited to Aesop, a storyteller who lived in ancient Greece about 2,500 years ago.

media.credit: Markus Knöll fontsaenger · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Markus Knöll fontsaenger

questions.description: A green grump who has a problem with holiday cheer.
questions.question: In the Dr. Seuss story of how the Grinch stole Christmas, what is the name of the Grinch's dog?
hints: His name has just three letters.
The Grinch ties an antler to his head so he can pull the sleigh like a reindeer.
His name is also a short form of Maximilian.
questions.fun_fact: At the end of the story, the Grinch's heart grows three sizes in one day.

media.credit: Bim24 · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bim24

questions.description: A spider with better handwriting than most doctors.
questions.question: I'm a spider who writes words like “Some Pig” in my web to save my friend Wilbur. Who wrote my story?
hints: The book is called “Charlotte's Web” and came out in 1952.
The author was American and wrote for The New Yorker magazine for many years.
His first two initials stand for Elwyn Brooks.
questions.fun_fact: E. B. White kept animals on his own farm in Maine, and a real barn spider inspired Charlotte.

media.credit: Luc Viatour · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Luc Viatour

questions.description: The smallest member of the family, and not just because he's the youngest.
questions.question: Stuart Little is born to a human family in New York, is only about 5 cm (2 in) tall and sails a toy boat in Central Park. What is he?
hints: He has fur and a long tail.
The family cat, Snowbell, is not happy about him.
Cats like to chase this little animal.
questions.fun_fact: In the 1999 film, Stuart's voice was played by Michael J. Fox.

media.credit: David McSpadden from Daly City, United States · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: David McSpadden from Daly City, United States

questions.description: A swap deal that no lawyer would ever approve.
questions.question: I'm a young mermaid who wants legs to walk on land. To get them, I give away my voice. Who do I give it to?
hints: It's someone who lives deep in the sea and does magic.
In the Disney film, she has tentacles like an octopus.
Her name in the film is Ursula.
questions.fun_fact: A bronze statue of the Little Mermaid has sat on a rock in Copenhagen, Denmark, since 1913.

media.credit: Toby Hudson · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Toby Hudson

questions.description: Fairy-tale real estate: lovely locations, very strange building materials.
questions.question: “The Three Little Pigs” is to a brick house as “Hansel and Gretel” is to a…
hints: The children are very hungry when they find it.
The story is a German fairy tale written down by two brothers.
It is made of sweets and cake.
questions.fun_fact: The story was published by the Brothers Grimm in Germany in 1812.

media.credit: F R · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: F R

questions.description: A shepherd with a very bad sense of humor.
questions.question: “The Tortoise and the Hare” warns against showing off. “The Boy Who Cried Wolf” warns against…
hints: The boy shouts for help again and again as a joke.
When the wolf really comes, nobody believes him.
He kept saying things that were not true.
questions.fun_fact: The expression “to cry wolf”, meaning to give a false alarm, comes from this fable.

media.credit: Bill Boaden · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bill Boaden

questions.description: A reality show where nobody wants to win the casting call.
questions.question: In “The Hunger Games”, each district sends one boy and one girl. How many players enter the arena each year?
hints: Katniss volunteers to take her younger sister's place.
It's an even number between 20 and 30.
Katniss's home, District 12, is the last district; double it.
questions.fun_fact: Suzanne Collins said the idea came from switching TV channels between a reality show and war news.

media.credit: USFWS Mountain Prairie · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: USFWS Mountain Prairie

questions.description: A knobbly root with a spicy temper and a sweet side at Christmas.
questions.question: This root spices many Christmas cookies and cakes. What is it?
hints: It is also used in Asian cooking and tea.
Its taste is warm and a bit hot.
A famous Christmas cookie is shaped like a little man and named after it.
questions.fun_fact: Ginger is not really a root: it is an underground stem called a rhizome.

media.credit: Sanjay Acharya (Sanjay ach at en.wikipedia) · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Sanjay Acharya (Sanjay ach at en.wikipedia)

questions.description: The only delivery drivers with antlers and no license.
questions.question: We have antlers, and on Christmas Eve we fly across the sky pulling something heavy. What do we pull?
hints: It is full of presents.
It glides on snow like a sled.
Santa Claus rides in it.
questions.fun_fact: In real life, reindeer can't fly, but they can swim very well and travel huge distances.

media.credit: Vojife · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Vojife

questions.description: A countdown clock made of pine branches and wax.
questions.question: Families light one more candle on this wreath each week. What is it counting down?
hints: It starts in late November or early December.
There are four candles, one for each week.
The season is called Advent.
questions.fun_fact: The first Advent wreath, made in Hamburg, Germany, in 1839, was a cartwheel with 24 candles.

media.credit: Rikky_Satin · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Rikky_Satin

questions.description: The oldest star of the ring, and it never forgets to take a bow.
questions.question: Which animal is performing in this circus ring?
hints: It can gallop very fast.
It wears metal shoes on its hooves.
Cowboys and knights ride it.
questions.fun_fact: The circus ring is round partly because it helps riders stay balanced while standing on a galloping horse.

media.credit: Jorge Royan · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jorge Royan

questions.description: The heroes of the circus that nobody ever claps for.
questions.question: In old traveling circuses, what was the main job of the big crew of hired laborers?
questions.answer: Putting up and taking down the big tent
wrong_answers: Warming up the crowd before the show
hints: Their work was done before the audience arrived and after it left.
They needed ropes, stakes and big hammers.
Without them, the show would happen under the open sky.
questions.fun_fact: These workers, called “roustabouts” in English, drove tent stakes into the ground by hand, swinging their sledgehammers one after another in a steady rhythm.

media.credit: Tyne & Wear Archives & Museums · No restrictions · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tyne & Wear Archives & Museums

questions.description: This performer would win any staring contest in town.
questions.question: I stand still for hours in the street, painted silver or gold, and only move when you drop a coin. Who am I?
hints: You'll find me in busy squares and streets.
I try not to blink.
Some people walk past thinking I'm made of bronze.
questions.fun_fact: Las Ramblas in Barcelona once had so many living statues that the city made them get permits.

media.credit: Jorge Láscar from Melbourne, Australia · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jorge Láscar from Melbourne, Australia

questions.description: The circus performer the crew calls when the piano needs moving.
questions.question: A juggler is to balls as a circus strongman is to…
hints: Think about who lifts heavy things.
He often has a big mustache and a striped or leopard-print suit.
It's a bar with a heavy weight on each end.
questions.fun_fact: Old strongmen's round globe barbells were often hollow, so they could be filled with sand or lead shot to change the weight.

media.credit: Dirk Annemans · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dirk Annemans

questions.description: Dragons do it naturally; humans need years of practice.
questions.question: What is the torch in this performer's hand for?
hints: The flame doesn't come from inside the performer's body.
The performer blows a fine mist out of the mouth.
The mist only catches fire when it meets a flame.
questions.fun_fact: Fire breathers say the golden rule is never to breathe in during the trick.

media.credit: uniquelycat (Cathy) Smith from USA · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: uniquelycat (Cathy) Smith from USA

questions.description: Sitting on a chair for hours, but make it an Olympic dream.
questions.question: “I'm video games played in competitions, with pro teams, coaches, packed arenas and big prize money.” What am I called?
hints: Fans can watch me live online or in huge stadiums.
My pros train for hours every day, just like athletes.
It's the word for sports, with an “e” in front.
questions.fun_fact: Big esports finals have filled stadiums with tens of thousands of fans, with millions more watching online.

media.credit: PantheraLeo1359531 · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: PantheraLeo1359531

questions.description: Two small controllers that never fight over who's left and who's right.
questions.question: These little controllers slide on and off the sides of a console. Which console family are they from?
hints: The console can be played on the TV or in your hands.
Its maker also created Mario.
Its name means to change from one thing to another.
questions.fun_fact: A pair of Joy-Con can be split so two players each hold one sideways as their own small controller.

media.credit: Crisco 1492 · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Crisco 1492

questions.description: The reason so many TVs have a crack shaped like a tennis swing.
questions.question: You swing a white remote like a tennis racket and your player on the TV swings too. In which decade did this first arrive in homes?
hints: Phones with touch screens were just becoming popular then.
The console that came with it had a very short name.
The Wii came out in 2006.
questions.fun_fact: So many people let go of the Wii remote mid-swing that Nintendo made the wrist strap thicker.

media.credit: Shixart1985 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Shixart1985

questions.description: Five is the number, and fun is the game.
questions.question: The console PS5 has a short name. What does the “PS” stand for?
hints: Its maker is the company Sony.
Its controller's four buttons are marked with a triangle, circle, cross and square.
The same name has been on every Sony home console since 1994, and its logo shows a P and an S.
questions.fun_fact: The first PlayStation came out in Japan in 1994, so the PS5 is the fifth main console of the family.

media.credit: Vu Hoang · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Vu Hoang

questions.description: A console with a number in its name that wasn't the year, the price or the players.
questions.question: Which of these games was NOT released on the Nintendo 64?
wrong_answers: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time
hints: The Nintendo 64 came out in 1996.
One of these games came out on the console after it.
That game takes Mario to a sunny island on the GameCube.
questions.fun_fact: The Nintendo 64 used cartridges instead of CDs, which made games load almost instantly.

media.credit: Evan-Amos · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Evan-Amos

questions.description: A controller named after something you should never swing around the living room.
questions.question: This Wii add-on is named after a martial arts weapon. Which film star made that weapon world-famous?
hints: The weapon is two sticks joined by a short chain or rope.
The star was a kung fu legend of the 1970s.
He starred in “Enter the Dragon”.
questions.fun_fact: The Nunchuk got its name from its shape: two parts joined by a cord, like the weapon.

media.credit: Evan-Amos · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Evan-Amos

questions.description: A detective who solves cases for clients with fur, feathers and scales.
questions.question: In which decade did Jim Carrey first star as Ace Ventura, the pet detective?
hints: This film made Jim Carrey a big movie star.
Jim Carrey also made “The Mask” that same year.
It was released in 1994.
questions.fun_fact: In the first film, Ace Ventura hunts for the missing dolphin mascot of the Miami Dolphins American football team.

media.credit: Giles Laurent · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Giles Laurent

questions.description: A man who traded his detective badge for a typewriter and never looked back.
questions.question: I was a real Pinkerton detective before I wrote “The Maltese Falcon” and created Sam Spade. Who am I?
hints: I'm an American writer, a father of “hard-boiled” crime fiction.
I also wrote “The Thin Man”, with the witty couple Nick and Nora Charles.
My first name starts with “Dash”.
questions.fun_fact: Hammett said many of his tough characters were based on real people he had met while working as a detective.

media.credit: Jorge Royan · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jorge Royan

questions.description: A village so peaceful you'd never guess how many crimes happen there.
questions.question: Which famous fictional detective lives in an English village like this one, called St. Mary Mead?
hints: She is an elderly lady who loves knitting and gardening.
She is an amateur: nobody pays her to solve crimes.
She was created by Agatha Christie.
questions.fun_fact: Agatha Christie said Miss Marple was partly inspired by her step-grandmother, who always expected the worst of people.

media.credit: Jeff Buck · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jeff Buck

questions.description: A tiny tornado that forgot to invite the storm clouds.
questions.question: Spinning columns like this one rise in deserts on hot days, even under a clear blue sky. What are they made of?
hints: The sun heats the ground first.
The ground then heats what is just above it.
Warm air goes up, spins, and picks up the dry ground with it.
questions.fun_fact: Dust devils also form on Mars, where NASA rovers have photographed them crossing the red plains.

media.credit: Steve Jurvetson · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Steve Jurvetson

questions.description: A lizard whose morning routine is just lying around, and it's allowed.
questions.question: Lizards like this one lie in the sun for hours every morning. Why do they do it?
hints: Mornings in the desert can be chilly.
Lizards can't make their own body heat like we can.
Without sunshine they would feel cold and slow.
questions.fun_fact: When an iguana gets too hot, it simply moves into the shade or hides under the ground.

media.credit: MusikAnimal · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: MusikAnimal

questions.description: Ancient Egypt's most famous guard has never once taken a lunch break.
questions.question: The Great Sphinx guards the pyramids of Giza. It is carved out of rock and has a human head. What animal's body does it have?
hints: It's a big animal from Africa.
It is a kind of cat.
People call it the king of the animals.
questions.fun_fact: The Great Sphinx is about 73 m (240 ft) long and was carved from a single ridge of limestone.

media.credit: Vyacheslav Argenberg · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Vyacheslav Argenberg

questions.description: A rock that went to the hairdresser and asked for “mushroom, please.”
questions.question: Over thousands of years, desert rocks like this one get a thin “stalk” and a wide top. What carved them?
hints: No water was needed for this job.
It works like sandpaper, very slowly.
The desert air carries tiny grains low over the ground.
questions.fun_fact: The stalk gets thinner because blown sand stays close to the ground, so it scrapes the bottom of the rock much more than the top.

media.credit: Asgalal · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Asgalal

questions.description: They wrapped their kings up like birthday presents, and it worked for thousands of years.
questions.question: Riddle: “We built the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing, next to the Nile, and we made mummies.” Who are we?
hints: We lived in a hot, sandy land in Africa.
Our kings were called pharaohs.
Our great pyramids still stand near Cairo.
questions.fun_fact: The Great Pyramid of Giza was the tallest building made by people for about 3,800 years.

media.credit: FuriousYogi · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: FuriousYogi

questions.description: This plant takes its time, then throws one giant party and says goodbye.
questions.question: Some agaves grow for decades, then shoot up one giant flower stalk just once and die. What nickname does this give them?
hints: The nickname is about a very long time.
It exaggerates how long the plant waits to bloom.
It's a word for 100 years.
questions.fun_fact: Despite the name, a century plant usually flowers after 10 to 30 years, and its stalk can grow up to 8 m (26 ft) tall.

media.credit: Randal · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Randal

questions.description: The only plant that goes on road trips without a car.
questions.question: In dry lands, plants like this one break off at the base and roll away in the wind. Why do they do it?
hints: The plant is already dead and dry when it rolls.
It's about making new plants.
Every bounce drops something small along the way.
questions.fun_fact: The tumbleweed famous from Wild West films is not American: it came from Russia in the 1870s, hidden in imported seeds.

questions.description: A greeting where saying hello is all about the angle.
questions.question: In Japan, people greet each other with a quick, polite bow. About how far do they bend forward for an everyday hello?
hints: Japanese workers and students learn several kinds of bow for different situations.
Deeper bows are kept for big apologies and big thanks.
It's less than half of a right angle.
questions.fun_fact: For a big thank-you or a sorry, people in Japan bow deeper, to about 30 or 45 degrees.

media.credit: Benh LIEU SONG (Flickr) · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Benh LIEU SONG (Flickr)

questions.description: The pharaohs would need subtitles to chat in Cairo today.
questions.question: Ancient Egyptians wrote in hieroglyphs. Egypt's official language today arrived about 1,400 years ago with armies from where?
hints: It's a big desert land east of the Red Sea.
Mecca is there.
The language's name sounds like this place.
questions.fun_fact: A descendant of the ancient Egyptian language, Coptic, is still used today in prayers in Egypt's Coptic churches.

media.credit: Vyacheslav Argenberg · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Vyacheslav Argenberg

questions.description: A hello you might hear right before a giraffe walks past.
questions.question: You're on safari and people greet you with “Jambo!”. In which country are you most likely to be?
hints: “Jambo” is a Swahili word.
Swahili is spoken in East Africa.
Its capital is Nairobi.
questions.fun_fact: The word “safari” comes from Swahili too: it means “journey”.

media.credit: eismcsquare · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: eismcsquare

questions.description: A word that left home long ago and always comes back.
questions.question: This throwing stick is called a “boomerang” in many languages. The word comes from the language of which people?
hints: These people have lived in their land for tens of thousands of years.
They are famous for very old rock art and for the didgeridoo.
Their land is home to kangaroos.
questions.fun_fact: Not every boomerang comes back: heavy hunting boomerangs were made to fly straight.

media.credit: A.Savin · FAL · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: A.Savin

questions.description: Animals speak one language, but people translate them very differently.
questions.question: Japanese children say one animal goes “kokekokko!”. What sound is that?
hints: This animal lives on a farm.
You hear it very early in the morning.
It's a bird with a red comb on its head.
questions.fun_fact: In Japan, a dog doesn't say “woof”: it says “wan wan”.

media.credit: STA3816 · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: STA3816

questions.description: The Vikings' language never died, it just moved somewhere very cold.
questions.question: Vikings spoke Old Norse. On one remote island it changed so little that people there can still read the old Viking sagas. Which language is it?
hints: The island is far out in the North Atlantic.
Vikings settled it around the year 870.
It's the island of geysers and volcanoes.
questions.fun_fact: Iceland has a committee that invents new Icelandic words, such as “tölva” for computer, from old words for “number” and “prophetess”.

media.credit: JIP · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: JIP

questions.description: A language nobody wrote down, yet billions speak its great-great-grandchildren.
questions.question: It was never written down. Linguists rebuilt it by comparing words like Sanskrit “pitar”, Latin “pater” and English “father”. What is it called?
hints: It was spoken roughly 6,000 years ago.
Its speakers may have lived on the steppes north of the Black Sea.
Its descendants range from India to Europe.
questions.fun_fact: Almost half of the world's people speak a language from this family, including Hindi, Spanish, English, Russian and Persian.

media.credit: Lucian Cioranu · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Lucian Cioranu

questions.description: The pointiest part of any big cat's smile.
questions.question: Eyes are to seeing as a wolf's fangs are to…
hints: Fangs are found in the mouth.
They are long, sharp teeth.
A wolf uses them to grab and hold its food.
questions.fun_fact: Your own pointy teeth next to the front ones are canines too, like a wolf's fangs, just much smaller.

media.credit: E L from Western-Finland · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: E L from Western-Finland

questions.description: A cat with a sword, a feather hat and the saddest eyes in movie history.
questions.question: You're watching “Shrek 2”. Cinderella is to glass slipper as Shrek's sword-fighting cat is to…
hints: Think of something he wears.
He wears them on his feet.
His name tells you what they are.
questions.fun_fact: The story of the clever cat in boots is much older than Shrek: Charles Perrault wrote it down in France in 1697.

media.credit: LauraDelga · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: LauraDelga

questions.description: A mammal that came to the party dressed as a knight.
questions.question: This American mammal has a shell of bony plates, digs burrows with strong claws, and one kind rolls into a ball. What is it?
hints: It lives only in the Americas, from Argentina to the southern United States.
Its armor has bands across its back.
Its name is Spanish for “little armored one”.
questions.fun_fact: The nine-banded armadillo almost always gives birth to four identical babies.

media.credit: USFWS Mountain-Prairie · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: USFWS Mountain-Prairie

questions.description: The very first restaurant every puppy, calf and baby visits.
questions.question: A dolphin, a bat and a cow are all called “mammals”. What does that word tell you about their babies?
hints: It's about what the babies eat.
The mother makes this food in her own body.
You can buy the cow's version at the supermarket.
questions.fun_fact: Seal mothers make milk so rich in fat that their pups can double their weight in a few days.

media.credit: Uberprutser · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Uberprutser

questions.description: An Ice Age smile that no dentist would ever want to fix.
questions.question: This skull belonged to an Ice Age hunter. Which animal was it?
hints: It was a meat-eating mammal.
It belongs to the cat family.
Look at those two long, blade-like teeth.
questions.fun_fact: The saber-toothed cat Smilodon could open its jaws wider than a lion, about 120 degrees.

media.credit: Wilfredor · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Wilfredor

questions.description: The farm's loudest hee-haw, and it isn't a joke.
questions.question: A donkey's bray can be heard kilometers away. Their wild ancestors lived in deserts. Why do they bray so loudly?
questions.answer: To stay in touch with others far away
hints: It's about talking, not about the weather.
In the desert there's little food, so animals spread out.
They're calling to friends they can't see.
questions.fun_fact: A donkey brays both breathing in (the “hee”) and breathing out (the “haw”).

media.credit: Tracie Hall from Orange County, us · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tracie Hall from Orange County, us

questions.description: Some singers need a stage; this one just needs a hill.
questions.question: This wolf is howling. Why do wolves howl?
hints: It isn't about the night sky at all.
Wolves live and hunt in families.
It's a way of saying “I'm over here!”
questions.fun_fact: A wolf's howl can be heard up to about 10 km (6 miles) away on a quiet night.

media.credit: Kikimora mashenka · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Kikimora mashenka

questions.description: A wise mandrill whose name is also his job description.
questions.question: In “The Lion King”, a wise mandrill holds baby Simba high above the animals. His name is Swahili. What does it mean?
hints: It's not about his looks or his brains.
Think of what he is to Mufasa and Simba.
It's what you call someone you trust and like.
questions.fun_fact: Many Lion King names are Swahili: Simba means “lion” and Pumbaa roughly means “silly”.

media.credit: David Octavian · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: David Octavian

questions.description: A tiny chef with a long tail and a big appetite for winning.
questions.question: This rodent is first in the Chinese zodiac, has a long bare tail, and Remy the Pixar chef is one. What animal is it?
hints: It's bigger than its round-eared little cousin.
In the legend, it won the zodiac race by riding on an ox.
It's the mouse's bigger, larger-toothed relative that people often spot in sewers and city streets.
questions.fun_fact: Rats laugh when tickled, with squeaks too high for people to hear.

media.credit: Dileep Kaluaratchie · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dileep Kaluaratchie

questions.description: The engine that runs on cuddles and never needs fuel.
questions.question: You're stroking a cat on your lap. A happy dog wags its tail as a happy cat…
hints: It's a quiet sound.
It sounds like a tiny motor.
It goes “rrrrrr”.
questions.fun_fact: Cats can purr while breathing in and breathing out, so the sound never stops.

media.credit: myllissa from Seoul, S. Korea · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: myllissa from Seoul, S. Korea

questions.description: Tiny but proud: the unit that tells your cereal box how much fun is inside.
questions.question: It measures how heavy something is, a paperclip weighs about one, and food labels list sugar and fat in it. What is it?
hints: It is a unit of mass, not of length or time.
Its symbol is a single lowercase letter.
A thousand of them make one kilogram.
questions.fun_fact: A US dollar bill and a euro banknote each weigh about one gram.

media.credit: Tdlnx · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tdlnx

questions.description: Same digit, different seat, wildly different paycheck.
questions.question: In the number 3,482,915, how much is the digit 8 worth?
hints: Count the places from the right: ones, tens, hundreds…
The 8 is the fifth digit from the right.
It sits in the ten-thousands place.
questions.fun_fact: The Romans had no place value: in Roman numerals, X means ten wherever you put it.

media.credit: Aliva Sahoo · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Aliva Sahoo

questions.description: A number so big it needs a whole parade of round friends behind it.
questions.question: How many zeros do you write in the number one million?
hints: One thousand has 3 zeros.
A million is a thousand thousands.
It is twice as many zeros as one thousand has.
questions.fun_fact: If you counted one number every second without stopping, reaching a million would take more than 11 days.

media.credit: Armin Kleiner · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Armin Kleiner

questions.description: A breakfast puzzle for people who like their eggs sorted.
questions.question: Counting 1 and 12 itself, how many whole numbers divide these 12 eggs into equal groups with none left over?
hints: Try groups of 1, 2, 3 and keep going.
Groups of 5 don't work: you'd have eggs left over.
The numbers are 1, 2, 3, 4, … and two more.
questions.fun_fact: 12 has more divisors than any smaller number, which is one reason eggs, hours and months come in twelves.

media.credit: Famartin · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Famartin

questions.description: Bees: tiny architects who never went to architecture school.
questions.question: You're looking at a honeycomb from a beehive. About how wide is one of its six-sided cells?
hints: Each cell is home for one baby bee.
A bee must fit inside, but only just.
It is about as wide as a pencil's eraser.
questions.fun_fact: Six-sided cells let bees store the most honey while using the least wax.

media.credit: Ark. Agricultural Experiment Station · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ark. Agricultural Experiment Station

questions.description: A pack of paper friends that loves being shuffled around.
questions.question: A standard deck of playing cards with hearts, spades, diamonds and clubs, without jokers: how many cards does it have?
hints: There are four suits.
Each suit runs from ace to king: 13 cards.
It is the same as the number of weeks in a year.
questions.fun_fact: There are so many ways to shuffle 52 cards that a well-shuffled deck is almost surely in an order no one has ever seen before.

media.credit: BlakeMagic · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: BlakeMagic

questions.description: Math has lots of number clubs, and this one has members in every elevator.
questions.question: Ancient Chinese counting rods showed them in black, winter thermometers often show them, and elevators use them for basement floors. What are they?
hints: Think of a very cold day in Siberia.
They sit on the left side of zero on a number line.
They are written with a minus sign in front.
questions.fun_fact: For centuries, many European mathematicians called negative numbers “absurd” and refused to use them.

media.credit: Oto Zapletal · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Oto Zapletal

questions.description: Two numbers walk into a map and say “you are here.”
questions.question: Sailors, pilots and phone maps all use a pair of numbers called latitude and longitude. What are they for?
questions.answer: Finding an exact place on Earth
wrong_answers: Measuring how deep the sea is
hints: Think of the lines drawn on a globe.
GPS gives you these two numbers.
One says how far north or south, the other how far east or west.
questions.fun_fact: Latitude was easy for old sailors to find from the stars, but longitude needed very accurate clocks, invented only in the 1700s.

media.credit: Henry James · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Henry James

questions.description: The die that always rolls under the sofa right when it's your turn.
questions.question: You roll a die and it shows 6 dots. What kind of number is 6?
hints: Try putting the dots in pairs.
No dot is left alone.
2, 4, 6 and 8 all belong to this group.
questions.fun_fact: Every whole number ending in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8 is even, however big it is.

media.credit: Mshuang2 · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Mshuang2

questions.description: The math lesson everyone suddenly pays attention to: pizza day.
questions.question: This pizza is cut into equal slices. What fraction of the whole pizza is one slice?
hints: Count the slices.
The bottom number is how many slices there are in total.
Half of the pizza is four slices.
questions.fun_fact: The word “fraction” comes from the Latin “fractus”, meaning “broken”.

media.credit: igorovsyannykov · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: igorovsyannykov

questions.description: Same cake, more slices, nobody gets any extra.
questions.question: 1/2 is to 2/4 as 1/3 is to…
hints: 2/4 is the same amount as 1/2.
Multiply the top and the bottom by the same number.
The bottom number is 6.
questions.fun_fact: Every fraction has infinitely many equivalent fractions: 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6 = 4/8, and so on forever.

media.credit: Acabashi · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Acabashi

questions.description: Cookies: the only thing more fun to count than sheep.
questions.question: How many cookies are on this plate?
hints: Look very carefully.
Count only what you can really see.
It is the number for “nothing at all”.
questions.fun_fact: Mathematicians in India were among the first to treat zero as a real number, more than 1,000 years ago.

media.credit: Stock Catalog · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Stock Catalog

questions.description: The fanciest window shopping you'll ever do, and nothing is for sale.
questions.question: Look at this glass box in a museum. What is it mainly for?
questions.answer: Protecting the objects from hands and dust
wrong_answers: Keeping the objects cold like a fridge
hints: The objects inside are old and precious.
Many visitors would love to pick them up.
It stops fingers and dirt from reaching them.
questions.fun_fact: Many museum cases also control the air inside, keeping it at a steady dampness so old wood, paper and cloth don't crack or rot.

media.credit: יעקב · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: יעקב

questions.description: The only place where the night starts whenever someone buys a ticket.
questions.question: I have a round ceiling, and when my lights go out, a machine paints stars and planets across it, even at noon. What am I?
hints: You visit me sitting down, often in a reclining seat.
My sky is not real: it is projected.
My name comes from the word “planet”.
questions.fun_fact: The first modern planetarium projector was shown in 1923 at the Deutsches Museum in Munich, Germany.

media.credit: Chad Ajamian · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Chad Ajamian

questions.description: A museum so big it took two decades to finish, right next door to some very old neighbors.
questions.question: The Grand Egyptian Museum near the Giza pyramids opened fully in 2025. It is the first to show all the treasures of which pharaoh together?
hints: He became pharaoh as a child.
His tomb was found almost untouched in 1922.
His golden mask is one of the most famous objects in the world.
questions.fun_fact: More than 5,000 objects were found in Tutankhamun's tomb, including chariots, sandals and even boxes of food.

media.credit: Ludovic Delot · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ludovic Delot

questions.description: A place where the countdown always ends with a very loud goodbye.
questions.question: It is the only place on Earth from which people have launched to the Moon, Space Shuttles took off here, and visitors can see a real Saturn V rocket. Where is it?
hints: It is in the United States.
It lies on the coast of Florida.
It is named after a US president who promised to reach the Moon.
questions.fun_fact: The Saturn V on show there is about 110 m (363 ft) long, and it is so big it lies on its side inside a whole building of its own.

media.credit: NASA Kennedy Space Center / NASA · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: NASA Kennedy Space Center / NASA

questions.description: The worst night shift ever: the dinosaur wants to play fetch.
questions.question: In the film “Night at the Museum”, a magic golden tablet brings the exhibits to life every night. Who did the tablet first belong to?
hints: He ruled a kingdom thousands of years ago.
In the film he is a young king who wakes up and helps the night guard.
Think of pyramids.
questions.fun_fact: The film is set in the real American Museum of Natural History in New York, which saw more visitors after the movie came out.

media.credit: Vicpeters · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Vicpeters

questions.description: Four peace champions walk into a quiz, and one of them took a very long flight to get here.
questions.question: Which of these Nobel Peace Prize winners is NOT from Africa?
hints: Three of them come from Ghana, Kenya and South Africa.
The odd one out comes from Asia.
She spent about 15 years under house arrest in Myanmar.
questions.fun_fact: Aung San Suu Kyi won the prize in 1991 but could only give her Nobel speech in Oslo 21 years later, in 2012.

media.credit: Sean Hayford O'Leary · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Sean Hayford O'Leary

questions.description: Before there was Macondo, there was a county nobody could spell.
questions.question: The writer in this photo created Macondo, inspired by an invented county in Mississippi. Which American Nobel winner invented that county?
hints: The invented county is called Yoknapatawpha.
He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1949.
He wrote “The Sound and the Fury”.
questions.fun_fact: Faulkner drew his own map of Yoknapatawpha County and signed it as its “sole owner and proprietor”.

media.credit: Festival Internacional de Cine en Guadalajara · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Festival Internacional de Cine en Guadalajara

questions.description: The most exclusive book club in the world, and you can't just bring a friend.
questions.question: How many chairs does the Swedish Academy, which picks the Nobel Prize in Literature, have?
hints: It's a small group, not a big parliament.
Members usually keep their chair for life.
It's more than a dozen but fewer than twenty.
questions.fun_fact: King Gustav III founded the Swedish Academy in 1786, more than 100 years before the first Nobel Prize.

media.credit: Bengt Nyman · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bengt Nyman

questions.description: A Caribbean poet who gave Homer a beach holiday.
questions.question: I was born on the island of Saint Lucia, wrote the long poem “Omeros” inspired by Homer, and won the 1992 Nobel Prize in Literature. Who am I?
hints: I wrote in English and also loved to paint.
My poem gives Homer's heroes' names to fishermen in a Caribbean village.
My first name is Derek.
questions.fun_fact: Tiny Saint Lucia has two Nobel winners, Derek Walcott and the economist Arthur Lewis, and both were born on January 23.

media.credit: Jayen466 · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jayen466

questions.description: The body's shape-shifters: they haven't decided what to be when they grow up.
questions.question: Cells like these can become almost any kind of cell in the body. In 2012, a Nobel went to turning adult cells back into them. What are they?
hints: Every baby starts out made of these cells.
Shinya Yamanaka from Japan won the prize for making them in the lab.
Doctors hope to use them to grow new tissue to repair damaged hearts, spines or other organs.
questions.fun_fact: Yamanaka needed just four genes to turn an ordinary skin cell back into a stem cell.

media.credit: NIH Image Gallery from Bethesda, Maryland, USA · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: NIH Image Gallery from Bethesda, Maryland, USA

questions.description: An ancient cough that finally met its detective.
questions.question: Robert Koch won the 1905 Nobel Prize for finding the germ behind it. It mainly attacks the lungs, and the BCG vaccine protects against it. What disease is it?
hints: It has been found in Egyptian mummies.
In the 1800s, patients were sent to mountain sanatoriums to breathe fresh air.
Its old name was “consumption”, and a constant cough with blood was its classic sign.
questions.fun_fact: March 24, the day Koch announced his discovery in 1882, is now World Tuberculosis Day.

media.credit: Daderot · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Daderot

questions.description: The best lab mistake since someone forgot to wash a Petri dish.
questions.question: A plastic that conducts electricity, which won the 2000 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, was found when a researcher added too much catalyst. About how many times too much?
hints: It happened in Hideki Shirakawa's lab in Japan.
Instead of a black powder, a shiny silver film appeared.
The mix-up was probably between millimoles and moles.
questions.fun_fact: Conducting polymers are now used in some phone screens and flexible OLED displays.

media.credit: Belikov Maxim · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Belikov Maxim

questions.description: The family recipe your parents passed on without asking you.
questions.question: You got half of it from your mom and half from your dad, it's shaped like a twisted ladder, and it's why you look like your family. What is it?
hints: It's inside almost every cell of your body.
Police can use it to find out who was at a place.
Its name is three letters long.
questions.fun_fact: Watson, Crick and Wilkins won the 1962 Nobel Prize in Medicine for working out DNA's twisted-ladder shape.

media.credit: Edward S. Curtis · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Edward S. Curtis

questions.description: The biggest group project in the world, and everyone wants to talk at once.
questions.question: The United Nations, which won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2001, meets in this hall. How many member countries does it have?
hints: Almost every country in the world is a member.
The newest member, South Sudan, joined in 2011.
The number is just under 200.
questions.fun_fact: The UN shared the 2001 Peace Prize with its Secretary-General Kofi Annan, and its agencies have won it many more times.

media.credit: Basil D Soufi · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Basil D Soufi

questions.description: A very long fishing trip, and the fish is not even the one telling the story.
questions.question: Ernest Hemingway's “The Old Man and the Sea” tells of a fisherman who sails out from this country. Which one is it?
hints: It's in the Caribbean Sea.
It's the largest island in the Caribbean.
Its capital is Havana.
questions.fun_fact: Hemingway lived near Havana for about 20 years, and the book helped him win the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1954.

media.credit: W.carter · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: W.carter

questions.description: An address in the middle of the sea, with no neighbors and a helicopter instead of a bus.
questions.question: “I stand on giant legs far out at sea. I drill deep into the seabed, and workers live on me for weeks.” What am I?
hints: I help get something out from under the ground.
What I bring up is used to make fuel for cars.
What I pump up from under the sea is thick, black and sticky.
questions.fun_fact: Norway's Troll A platform is taller than the Eiffel Tower, measured from the seabed to its top.

media.credit: Socket0 · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Socket0

questions.description: A puppet with a lying problem and a very bad day at sea.
questions.question: His nose grows when he lies, and in the Disney film he finds his father inside a giant whale. What is this puppet made of?
hints: His story was first written in Italy.
The same material is used to make pencils and chopsticks.
He was carved from a log.
questions.fun_fact: In Carlo Collodi's original 1883 book, Pinocchio is swallowed by a giant shark, not a whale.

media.credit: Myriamdc · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Myriamdc

questions.description: A checkerboard that refuses to sit still, and the artist who should be blamed for it.
questions.question: I'm a Japanese artist. My 1977 book showed a disc of thin rectangles on a checkerboard of rectangles, and the disc seems to float and slide. Who am I?
hints: The famous illusion carries my family name.
My book was a collection of black-and-white patterns made for designers and artists.
The illusion is usually called the “… disc” after my surname, which starts with O.
questions.fun_fact: Scientists still argue about why the Ouchi disc seems to wobble, but small eye movements seem to play a big part.

media.credit: Theo van Doesburg · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Theo van Doesburg

questions.description: Your drink is fine, it's the physics that's broken.
questions.question: I make a straw in a glass of water look broken. I bend light when it passes from water into air. Glasses and lenses use me too. What am I?
hints: I'm not a mirror trick: I happen when light goes through something.
I'm also why a pool looks shallower than it really is.
A prism uses me to split white light into a rainbow.
questions.fun_fact: Light travels about 25% slower in water than in air, and that change of speed is what bends it.

media.credit: Shixart1985 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Shixart1985

questions.description: A twig that went for a walk.
questions.question: Stick insects look just like little twigs. How many legs does a stick insect have?
hints: Don't count by how it looks: think about what kind of animal it is.
It has the same number as an ant or a bee.
All insects have this many legs.
questions.fun_fact: Some stick insects sway gently back and forth as they walk, like a twig moving in the wind.

media.credit: Dcrjsr · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dcrjsr

questions.description: The world champion of hide-and-seek, who never actually hides very well.
questions.question: I wear glasses, a hat with a pom-pom and a red-and-white striped shirt. I hide in huge, busy pictures full of people. Who am I?
hints: I appear in big books where you have to search every page.
My friends include a wizard and a dog whose tail you can spot.
Readers always ask “Where's…?” before my name.
questions.fun_fact: The British illustrator Martin Handford created the striped hider in 1987, and his name changes in different countries.

media.credit: Aviv Ben Or vivanebro · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Aviv Ben Or vivanebro

questions.description: An animal that can't decide if it wants to quack or eat carrots.
questions.question: A drawing printed in a German magazine in 1892 shows a duck or a rabbit, depending on how you look. The duck's bill becomes the rabbit's what?
hints: The duck faces one way and the rabbit faces the other.
The bill sticks out long and thin from the head.
On a rabbit, they're the longest part of the head.
questions.fun_fact: The philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein made the duck–rabbit famous by using it to ask what it really means to “see” something.

media.credit: Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bentham-Moxon Trust.; Curtis, William; Curtis's botanical magazine dedications, 1827-1927 : portraits and biographical notes.; Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew.; Stanley Smith Horticultural Trust.

questions.description: One director to rule them all.
questions.question: I'm a film director from New Zealand. I filmed a trilogy about a magic ring there, using camera tricks to make grown actors look tiny. Who am I?
