questions.question: You're watching the 1969 film “Battle of Britain”: its German fighters are Spanish-built Bf 109 copies. Which engine powers them?
hints: Spain built the planes long after the war, when German engines were scarce.
The engine is British.
It also powered the Spitfire, the Bf 109's old rival.
questions.fun_fact: The Spanish version was nicknamed “Buchón”, meaning pouter pigeon, because of the bulge under its nose.

media.credit: Daderot · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Daderot

questions.description: A big cat that ate fuel instead of meat.
questions.question: This heavy tank of World War II had an 88 mm gun, very thick armor and the name of a big cat. Which country built it?
hints: Its maker also built a tank named Panther.
Its gun was based on the famous “eighty-eight”, which first served as an anti-aircraft gun.
The firms Henschel and Porsche designed versions of it.
questions.fun_fact: Tiger 131, captured in Tunisia in 1943, is one of the very few Tiger tanks that can still drive today.

media.credit: Signal Corps Archive from United States · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Signal Corps Archive from United States

questions.description: Proof that a big mess at a factory can end up cleaning up your mess at home.
questions.question: When you wipe up a spill with a paper towel, you use the fix for a 1907 mistake: a load of paper too thick to become what?
hints: The paper was meant to be soft and thin.
Its company already made a product for one room in the house.
You find a roll of it in every bathroom.
questions.fun_fact: The Scott Paper Company cut the too-thick paper into sheets and sold them as “Sani-Towels”.

media.credit: Work With Sounds · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Work With Sounds

questions.description: The only drawing that a good shake can make vanish forever.
questions.question: You twist two knobs to draw lines on a gray screen, then shake the toy to wipe it clean. In which decade did it first go on sale?
hints: Your grandparents could have played with one as kids.
It has no batteries and no screen with pixels.
It came out in the same decade as the first person in space.
questions.fun_fact: A French electrician, André Cassagnes, got the idea when pencil marks showed through a sheet coated with aluminum powder.

media.credit: Les Chatfield · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Les Chatfield

questions.description: Fashion designers would never put these on a runway, no matter how bold they feel.
questions.question: What are these for?
hints: You use them where you get wet.
They work like the feet of a frog or a duck.
Divers wear them in the sea.
questions.fun_fact: Benjamin Franklin made wooden fins for his hands when he was about 11 years old.

media.credit: Helmardine · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Helmardine

questions.description: A smelly kitchen accident that later rolled onto every road in the world.
questions.question: Charles Goodyear made rubber strong and stretchy when a rubber and sulfur mix touched a hot stove. In which year did that happen?
hints: Bicycle and car tires came only after this discovery.
Queen Victoria had only just begun her reign.
It happened about 50 years before the first car.
questions.fun_fact: The Goodyear tire company was named after him in 1898, but he and his family had nothing to do with it.

media.credit: Naturpuur · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Naturpuur

questions.description: A color so loud it practically shouts from the test tube.
questions.question: Fuchsine, a bright pink-purple dye, was patented in 1859 by a French chemist in a city famous for its silk weavers. Which city?
hints: The city lies in the east of France.
It is where two rivers meet, the Rhône and the Saône.
It is France's third-largest city, known for its food.
questions.fun_fact: The same dye was soon renamed “magenta” after a battle fought that year near the Italian town of Magenta.

media.credit: రహ్మానుద్దీన్ · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: రహ్మానుద్దీన్

questions.description: An egg's best friend in the frying pan.
questions.question: When you fry an egg in a non-stick pan, you can thank a chemist who found the coating by accident in 1938. Who was he?
hints: He worked for the American chemical company DuPont.
He was trying to make a new gas for refrigerators.
A gas tank seemed empty, but it was full of a slippery white powder.
questions.fun_fact: The coating, Teflon, is so slippery that almost nothing sticks to it, not even a gecko's feet.

media.credit: Horacio Cambeiro · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Horacio Cambeiro

questions.description: A tall, worried New Yorker who has never once been short of a view.
questions.question: In the film Madagascar, Melman is a giraffe. How many little horns does a giraffe usually have on top of its head?
hints: Picture Melman's head from the front.
It's fewer than three.
The same number as a giraffe has eyes.
questions.fun_fact: A giraffe's little horns are called ossicones, and they are covered in skin and hair.

media.credit: Tdorante10 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tdorante10

questions.description: A hippo who never learned to aim, so he just spreads it everywhere instead.
questions.question: Why does a male hippo spin his tail like a fan while he poops?
hints: It's a message for other hippos.
Other males smell it and get the idea.
It says “this stretch of river is mine”.
questions.fun_fact: Hippos also leave dung piles along the paths they use on land at night.

media.credit: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Diego Delso

questions.description: A snack on legs that refuses to be anyone's snack.
questions.question: About how fast can a Thomson's gazelle sprint when a cheetah chases it?
hints: Much faster than the fastest human.
As fast as a car on a country road.
Only a little slower than the cheetah itself.
questions.fun_fact: A gazelle can keep running much longer than a cheetah, which gets tired after a short sprint.

media.credit: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Diego Delso

questions.description: Pride Rock's loudest alarm clock.
questions.question: On safari at night, you hear a lion roar as mighty as Mufasa's. About how far away could that lion be?
hints: Much farther than a soccer field.
Farther than you could walk in an hour.
About 5 miles.
questions.fun_fact: Lions often roar at dusk and dawn to tell other prides whose land it is.

media.credit: Charles J. Sharp · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Charles J. Sharp

questions.description: The original spa day, no cucumber slices included.
questions.question: This warthog is rolling in mud. Besides cooling off, what does the dried mud protect it from?
hints: The danger is very small.
It's something that buzzes around its head.
Ticks and flies can't get through the crust.
questions.fun_fact: Warthogs often kneel on their front legs to eat grass, and they have hard pads there.

media.credit: Patrick Pelletier · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Patrick Pelletier

questions.description: A rule that, for once, almost the whole world agreed on.
questions.question: Ivory is the hard white material of elephant tusks, and old piano keys were covered in it. Why did the world ban the ivory trade in 1989?
wrong_answers: It is too heavy to ship
hints: It's about where ivory comes from.
Hunters wanted the tusks.
Fewer tusks sold means more elephants keep theirs.
questions.fun_fact: Today most piano keys are made of plastic instead of ivory.

media.credit: Shixart1985 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Shixart1985

questions.description: Behind every king is a very busy queen.
questions.question: Like Nala in The Lion King, this is a lioness. What is the main job lionesses do for their pride?
hints: It's about food.
They work as a team.
They sneak up on zebras and antelopes.
questions.fun_fact: Lionesses often hunt together, surrounding prey from different sides.

media.credit: Vanmulondo · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Vanmulondo

questions.description: A bird that got its own mummy before most people did.
questions.question: Ancient Egyptians linked this white bird with a black, curved bill to Thoth, god of writing, and mummified millions of them. What is it?
hints: It wades in marshes on long legs.
Thoth is often shown with this bird's head.
Its name says the Egyptians thought it was holy.
questions.fun_fact: Sacred ibises that escaped from zoos now live in the wild in France and Spain.

media.credit: Charles J. Sharp · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Charles J. Sharp

questions.description: The loudest summer guest, and it didn't even bring a speaker.
questions.question: I grow up underground for years, then climb a tree and leave my empty skin behind. In summer, the males sing very loudly. What am I?
hints: I am an insect with clear, see-through wings.
My song is a loud buzzing that comes from trees on hot days.
Some of my kind come out of the ground all together every 13 or 17 years.
questions.fun_fact: Some cicadas can be as loud as a lawn mower, and you can hear them from far away.

media.credit: Dietmar Rabich · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dietmar Rabich

questions.description: Part pig, part elephant, and fully ready for a swim.
questions.question: Look at this tapir. When it dives under water, what can it use its short trunk for?
hints: Tapirs often jump into rivers to hide from danger.
Thanks to its trunk, a tapir can stay hidden under water for a while.
The tip of the trunk can stay above the water.
questions.fun_fact: Tapirs look like pigs, but their closest living relatives are horses and rhinos.

media.credit: Giles Laurent · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Giles Laurent

questions.description: A monkey in a fluffy sweater, and the tropics didn't stop it.
questions.question: Woolly monkeys have thick soft fur, a tail that grips branches and wide nostrils that face sideways. To which group of primates do they belong?
hints: The group's name tells you where its members live.
All monkeys from Central and South America belong to it.
Europeans once called the Americas by this two-word name.
questions.fun_fact: No monkey from Africa or Asia has a tail that can grip; only some monkeys of the Americas have one.

media.credit: Hans Hillewaert · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Hans Hillewaert

questions.description: He went to measure the Earth and came back with a much longer trip.
questions.question: Which French scientist, after helping measure the Earth near the equator, made the first scientific trip down the Amazon River in 1743?
hints: His expedition worked in what is now Ecuador.
He made a map of the Amazon on the way.
He helped bring rubber and the poison curare to Europe's attention.
questions.fun_fact: La Condamine's group showed that the Earth is slightly flattened at the poles, as Isaac Newton had predicted.

media.credit: Alexander Gerst · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Alexander Gerst

questions.description: Smoke signals that nobody in the rainforest wanted to receive.
questions.question: Watch: most fires in the Amazon are lit by people on purpose. Why?
questions.answer: To clear land for farms and cattle
hints: Most of these fires happen in the dry season.
After the fire, the land looks very different.
Cows and crops need open fields.
questions.fun_fact: The Amazon rainforest is so wet that fires there rarely start by themselves.

media.credit: NOAA Satellites · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: NOAA Satellites

questions.description: A bug that skipped leg day and trained only its forehead.
questions.question: The male Hercules beetle has a huge horn that can be longer than the rest of its body. What does it mostly use it for?
hints: Females don't have this giant horn.
It matters most in the mating season.
The winner gets to meet a female.
questions.fun_fact: A Hercules beetle can carry many times its own weight, which is how it got the name of the strong Greek hero.

media.credit: Didier Descouens · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Didier Descouens

questions.description: A family vacation where the hotel has no roof and a lot of mosquitoes.
questions.question: In “Rio 2”, Blu, Jewel and their kids leave the city of Rio de Janeiro. Where do they fly to?
hints: They go looking for other wild blue macaws.
There, Jewel finds her long-lost father and a whole flock of macaws.
It's the biggest rainforest in the world.
questions.fun_fact: Blu is a Spix's macaw, a real species that died out in the wild and was later released again in Brazil.

media.credit: Wilfredor · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Wilfredor

questions.description: A tiny shot now saves you a very bad trip later.
questions.question: Travelers to the Amazon are often told to get a yellow fever vaccine. In which of these countries does yellow fever NOT occur?
hints: Yellow fever lives in the hot, wet parts of two continents.
The mosquito that spreads it lives in tropical forests on both sides of the Atlantic Ocean.
This country is in Asia, where the disease has never taken hold.
questions.fun_fact: Max Theiler won the 1951 Nobel Prize in Medicine for developing the yellow fever vaccine.

media.credit: Raimond Spekking · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Raimond Spekking

questions.description: Ancient farmers who were very, very serious about keeping their feet dry.
questions.question: Long ago, people built thousands of raised fields and mounds like these in the flooded Llanos de Mojos. In which country are they?
hints: The region is a seasonally flooded savanna in the southwest of the Amazon basin.
The Mamoré River, which later joins the Madeira, winds through these plains.
Its other famous landscapes include a giant salt flat and Lake Titicaca.
questions.fun_fact: Some of the forest islands in the Llanos de Mojos were made by people more than 10,000 years ago.

media.credit: Stéphen Rostain, Doyle McKey · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Stéphen Rostain, Doyle McKey

questions.description: Some explorers look for a lost city; some cities wait centuries to be found.
questions.question: You're standing among the ancient roads and ditches of Kuhikugu in Brazil's Xingu region. Which vanished British explorer may have been looking for a place like this?
hints: He disappeared in the Brazilian forest in 1925.
He called the lost city he was looking for by a single letter.
The 2016 film “The Lost City of Z” tells his story.
questions.fun_fact: Kuhikugu may once have been home to thousands of people, living in connected villages with roads and bridges.

media.credit: Amazônia Real from Manaus AM, Brasil · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Amazônia Real from Manaus AM, Brasil

questions.description: When the river won't take your boat where you want, just carry it over a mountain.
questions.question: In Werner Herzog's film “Fitzcarraldo”, a huge riverboat like this was really dragged over a hill. In which country was that filmed?
hints: The film's story starts in a rubber-boom city that you can't reach by road.
The hill lies between two rivers high up in the Amazon basin, close to the Andes.
Herzog filmed in the Andean country that is home to Machu Picchu.
questions.fun_fact: The crew really pulled a ship of over 300 tons over a hill, without special effects.

media.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Unknown authorUnknown author

questions.description: Three brothers walked into the jungle and came back with a plan the size of a small country.
questions.question: Orlando, Cláudio and Leonardo Villas-Bôas spent years in the Brazilian forest. What did their campaign help create in 1961?
hints: The brothers first reached the area on a government expedition in the 1940s.
It is a huge protected area in the state of Mato Grosso, bigger than some countries.
It is named after a river that flows north into the Amazon.
questions.fun_fact: More than a dozen different Indigenous peoples live together inside the Xingu park.

media.credit: Ben Sutherland · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ben Sutherland

questions.description: The original pea shooter, but with much better aim.
questions.question: A blowgun dart is thin as a skewer, the tube is wider, and hunters wrap a tuft of fluff around the dart's back end. What is the fluff for?
questions.answer: Sealing the tube behind the dart
wrong_answers: Holding the poison on the dart
Helping the dart float on water
Showing which hunter shot the dart
hints: Think about blowing through a straw with a loose pea inside.
The hunter fires with one short, hard puff into the tube.
It works like a plug.
questions.fun_fact: Some Amazon blowguns are about 3 m (10 ft) long, yet hunters can hit a bird high in the treetops.

media.credit: Zahidulla · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Zahidulla

questions.description: A forest pharmacy that never needed a shop sign.
questions.question: I'm an Amazon cousin of mahogany. My seeds give a bitter oil that people burn in candles and rub on skin to keep mosquitoes away. What am I?
hints: I'm a tall tree, not a palm.
My name comes from a Tupi word said to mean “bitter oil.”
My name starts with “Andi…”.
questions.fun_fact: Andiroba's scientific name is Carapa guianensis, and its oil is now used in soaps, creams and candles.

media.credit: Ivan Mlinaric · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ivan Mlinaric

questions.description: The party snack bowl, long before it ever reached the bowl.
questions.question: This close-up shows a juicy fruit from Brazil with a curved shell hanging below it. Which nut is inside that shell?
hints: In English, the juicy part is called an “apple.”
The nut is often eaten roasted and salted, and it's shaped like a letter C.
Cooks in India and Thailand toss it into curries and stir-fries.
questions.fun_fact: Cashews are never sold in their shell, because the shell holds an oil that irritates skin, like poison ivy.

media.credit: TNSE NEETHI VPM · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: TNSE NEETHI VPM

questions.description: Every forest breathes, but this one gets all the credit.
questions.question: What is the largest tropical rainforest on Earth, often called the “lungs of the world”?
hints: It grows around the river that carries the most water on Earth.
It's in South America.
Its river shares its name with a famous online shop.
questions.fun_fact: Despite the nickname, about half of the oxygen on Earth comes from tiny plankton in the oceans.

media.credit: Robert Kerton, CSIRO · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Robert Kerton, CSIRO

questions.description: A salad ingredient with a heart of gold, or at least a heart of white.
questions.question: Palm heart is a soft white vegetable eaten in salads. Where on the palm tree does it come from?
questions.answer: The tender core at the top of the stem
hints: It's not a fruit or a seed.
New leaves grow out of this part.
Cutting it out can kill a palm that has only one stem.
questions.fun_fact: Many farms grow the peach palm for palm heart, because it sprouts new stems and keeps producing after harvest.

media.credit: Chris Gorringe · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Chris Gorringe

questions.description: Ancient Amazon gardeners left behind dirt so good that scientists are still copying the recipe.
questions.question: Terra preta, the black Amazon soil made centuries ago with charcoal, inspired today's “biochar.” Besides helping crops, what is biochar meant to do?
hints: Think about climate change.
Charcoal is mostly carbon, and buried charcoal can last for centuries.
It keeps a greenhouse gas out of the air.
questions.fun_fact: Some terra preta made over 500 years ago is still so fertile that people in Brazil dig it up and sell it as potting soil.

media.credit: Rockwurm · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Rockwurm

questions.description: The biggest animal on land is also the best at waving hello.
questions.question: African elephants have the biggest ears of any animal. They flap them a lot, most of all on hot, sunny days. What does this help them do?
hints: Think about what you want on a really hot day.
The ears work a bit like a fan.
Lots of blood runs through the ears and loses heat there.
questions.fun_fact: One African elephant ear can be as big as a door, about 2 m (6 ft) tall.

media.credit: Bernard DUPONT · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bernard DUPONT

questions.description: A spider that always dresses for a fancy party: glossy black with a red badge.
questions.question: The black widow spider is shiny black, has a red hourglass mark and is very venomous. Where does the “widow” in its name come from?
questions.answer: The female sometimes eats the male
wrong_answers: It only comes out at funerals
It always lives alone in old houses
Its bite was first found on a widow
hints: It has to do with how the spider behaves, not with people.
A widow is a woman whose husband has died.
The female is much bigger than the male.
questions.fun_fact: Strand for strand, black widow silk is stronger than steel of the same thickness.

media.credit: Luc Viatour · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Luc Viatour

questions.description: An athlete who trains all summer in the tall grass.
questions.question: I'm green or brown and live in grassy fields. I sing by rubbing my back legs on my wings and jump about 20 times my length. Who am I?
hints: I am an insect with six legs.
My long back legs fold up like a pocketknife.
My cousins, the locusts, fly in huge swarms that can eat whole fields.
questions.fun_fact: Grasshoppers have ears on their bellies, just behind the back legs.

media.credit: Martin Vorel · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Martin Vorel

questions.description: A bat with a face like a bulldog and a voice like a rock concert.
questions.question: The greater bulldog bat catches fish with its claws, and its calls are among the loudest of any animal. Where does it live in the wild?
hints: It lives in the tropics, near rivers and coasts.
At night it flies low over calm water, using echoes to find fish near the surface.
Its range stretches from Mexico to Argentina.
questions.fun_fact: Its calls are so loud that, close up, they're about as loud as a jet engine, but they're too high-pitched for humans to hear.

media.credit: Juan Cruzado Cortés · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Juan Cruzado Cortés

questions.description: An animal that thinks walking is only for beginners.
questions.question: What is the biggest hopping animal in the world? It lives in Australia and carries its baby in a pouch.
hints: It has huge back feet and a long, strong tail.
Its baby is called a joey.
It appears on Australia's coat of arms, next to an emu.
questions.fun_fact: A red kangaroo can cover about 8 m (26 ft) in one single hop.

media.credit: John Robert McPherson · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: John Robert McPherson

questions.description: A stone hug so big that a whole crowd fits inside it.
questions.question: You stand in St. Peter's Square in Vatican City, wrapped by two huge curved arms of stone columns. About how many columns are there?
hints: There are four rows of columns side by side.
It is far more than you could count in a minute.
It is a few hundred.
questions.fun_fact: The colonnade has 284 columns, and from two special spots on the square the four rows line up so perfectly that they look like just one.

media.credit: Diliff · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Diliff

questions.description: Paris critics in 1900 judged architecture the same way they judged dinner.
questions.question: French critics mocked the curving, plant-like Art Nouveau of Hector Guimard with a food nickname. What was it?
hints: The nickname came from the long, wavy lines.
Think of something long that bends and curls.
It is usually served with sauce.
questions.fun_fact: Guimard made his name with the Castel Béranger, a Paris apartment building where he designed everything, down to the wallpaper and door handles.

media.credit: GFreihalter · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: GFreihalter

questions.description: Quasimodo's home was a building site long before it was his.
questions.question: Quasimodo's home in the Disney film is real: Notre-Dame in Paris. About how long did it take to build?
hints: Work started in the Middle Ages, with no engines or electricity.
Many of the first builders never saw it finished.
It took several lifetimes.
questions.fun_fact: Building started in 1163 and was finished around 1345, so more than 180 years later.

media.credit: Dietmar Rabich · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dietmar Rabich

questions.description: A painter who worked as if the sunflowers might wilt before he finished.
questions.question: If you lined up every painting Vincent van Gogh made in his roughly ten years as an artist, about how many would there be?
hints: He started painting late, in his late twenties.
Some weeks he finished more than one painting a day.
The number is close to a thousand.
questions.fun_fact: In his last 70 days, in the French village of Auvers, Van Gogh made about 70 paintings.

media.credit: Vincent van Gogh · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Vincent van Gogh

questions.description: Huge eyes, wild hair, and a sword taller than the hero.
questions.question: I come from Japan and I move. My characters often have huge eyes, and Studio Ghibli made me famous with “Spirited Away”. What am I?
hints: You watch me on a screen.
My printed, still cousin is read in books from right to left.
I am the Japanese word for animation.
questions.fun_fact: “Spirited Away” won the Oscar for Best Animated Feature in 2003.

media.credit: David Kernan · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: David Kernan

questions.description: The moment painters finally discovered that far-away things look small.
questions.question: In which century did Italian artists work out how to paint depth, with lines meeting at one vanishing point?
hints: It happened in Florence, a city full of rich art lovers.
The architect Brunelleschi showed it with a mirror and a painting.
Think of the 1400s.
questions.fun_fact: Around 1415, Brunelleschi proved his method with a painting of Florence's Baptistery, viewed through a hole and reflected in a mirror.

media.credit: Edanziger · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Edanziger

questions.description: Your sneakers, your phone and your cereal box all have one thing they love to show off.
questions.question: I'm small, but you see me on shoes, cars and phones. I'm a picture or design that tells you at once which company made something. What am I?
hints: I am not made of words you say out loud, like a catchy phrase.
Companies sometimes pay designers a fortune to draw me.
A bitten apple or a swoosh are famous examples of me.
questions.fun_fact: Many famous logos are simple on purpose, so you can still recognize them when they are tiny on a screen.

media.credit: Eric Fischer · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Eric Fischer

questions.description: Long before filters, every photo came with one setting: gray.
questions.question: The very first photographs ever taken were all in black and white. In which century were they made?
hints: It was before cars and airplanes.
A French inventor made the oldest one that still exists.
Think of the 1820s.
questions.fun_fact: The oldest surviving photo, taken by Nicéphore Niépce from his window around 1827, needed many hours of light to appear.

media.credit: Shixart1985 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Shixart1985

questions.description: Staring at yourself in the mirror for hours is just vanity, unless you're holding a paintbrush.
questions.question: This painting is a self-portrait. Who painted it?
hints: Look at the swirling brushstrokes in the background.
He was a Dutch painter who lived in France at the end of his life.
He also painted “Sunflowers”.
questions.fun_fact: Van Gogh painted more than 35 self-portraits, partly because he could not afford to pay models.

media.credit: Vincent van Gogh · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Vincent van Gogh

questions.description: Your thumbs are fast, but they are not always right.
questions.question: Phones like this one have autocorrect turned on while you type. What does autocorrect do?
questions.answer: It fixes misspelled words as you type
wrong_answers: It translates your message into another language
It reads your messages out loud
It sends your message later by itself
hints: It works while your fingers are still on the keyboard.
It is about typing mistakes.
Type “teh” and it quickly turns it into “the”.
questions.fun_fact: Autocorrect sometimes gets it wrong, and funny autocorrect mistakes have filled whole books and websites.

media.credit: Nenad Stojkovic · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Nenad Stojkovic

questions.description: It sits on the shelf all day, waiting for someone to say its name.
questions.question: Smart speakers wait for a wake word such as “Alexa” or “Hey Google”. What does the speaker do right after it hears it?
questions.answer: It starts listening to your request
hints: Before the word, it ignores what you say.
Its light often turns on to show it is ready.
Now you can ask it about the weather.
questions.fun_fact: The device listens for the wake word on its own chip, without sending your voice anywhere until it hears it.
